Dispersion of a reliability profile

Source: R/algebra-dispersion.R
kl_dispersion.Rd

kl_dispersion() computes the dispersion \(H\) of the site reliabilities around their informativeness \(I\), and kl_contributions() the term of each site, whose mean is \(H\).

Usage

kl_dispersion(S)

kl_contributions(S)

Arguments

S

Site reliabilities, a numeric vector of numbers strictly between 0 and 1, as returned by site_reliability().

Value

kl_dispersion() returns \(H\), a number of at least 0. kl_contributions() returns a numeric vector with one term for each site, with the names of S.

Details

The dispersion is the minimum of the average divergence that defines \(I\), $$H = \frac{1}{J}\sum_j \mathrm{KL}\{\mathrm{Ber}(I) \| \mathrm{Ber}(S_j)\} = \frac{1}{J}\sum_j A(m + \Delta_j) - A(m),$$ where \(A(t) = \log(1 + e^t)\), \(m\) is the logit of \(I\) and \(\Delta_j\) the centered logit of site \(j\) (Lee, 2026, Theorem 2 and Proposition 2). It is 0 only when all the reliabilities are equal.

A site's term is the divergence of \(I\) from the site's reliability. Removing the site would also move \(I\), so the term is not the change in \(H\) without that site.

References

Lee, J. (2026). The geometry of informativeness: A Bregman-centroid diagnostic for partial pooling in multisite trials. Unpublished manuscript.

See also

logit_moments() and local_terms() for the logit variance \(V\) and the second-order approximation \(H \approx I(1-I)V/2\).

Examples

S <- site_reliability(se = c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30), sigma_tau = 0.2)
kl_dispersion(S)
#> [1] 0.07569242
kl_contributions(S)
#> [1] 0.134361601 0.009963631 0.010239076 0.148205370
mean(kl_contributions(S))
#> [1] 0.07569242
